extracted.intended_audience: public company registrants, investors, auditors/assurance providers, and advisors/commenters on SEC climate-disclosure rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidentiary discussion on what climate-related information public companies should disclose (e.g., GHG emissions, risk disclosures), appropriate frameworks, timeliness, and assurance practices to enable investor use and comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recognized reporting frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: The TCFD, the SASB, the GRI, the Principles for Responsible Investment, the PCAF, and the CDP (among others) have all developed standards and systems that aim to help firms and investors identify, measure, and communicate climate-related information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple frameworks exist because each seeks to provide different information or fulfill different functions; registrants commonly align with one or more frameworks (statistics cited on adoption rates). The Corporate Reporting Dialogue and other efforts aim to promote coherence, consistency, and comparability between frameworks; alignment degrees with TCFD items range from Full to None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many registrants disclose Scope 1 and 2 emissions; evidence shows substantial but incomplete reporting across firms and by firm size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites statistics on adoption (e.g., percentages in Russell 1000 halves) and notes that registrants demonstrating measurement and disclosure processes plausibly have forthcoming disclosures not yet in datasets. The rules require some disclosure of GHG emissions to help investors understand registrants' risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of emissions disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions and sustainability disclosures are often published with substantial lags (commonly 12–18 months after fiscal year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late publication hinders investor knowledge; commenters and studies note that lack of clear timing standards for sustainability reports greatly hinders investor use. Timely reporting is important because emissions data can be out of date by the time it is published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and disclosure processes in place
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants that disclose Scope 1 and 2 emissions have demonstrated they have measurement and disclosure processes in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having processes in place indicates plausibility of forthcoming disclosures; registrants with processes are likely to be able to provide required emissions information when rules mandate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of generic/boilerplate disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantial fraction of registrants provide generic or boilerplate sustainability information that is of limited utility to the marketplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies (e.g., SASB 'State of Disclosure') report about 50% of registrants provide boilerplate disclosures; management discussions should be sufficiently precise and informative rather than generic to be useful to investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking climate-related disclosures to financial impacts (materiality focused on cash flows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures should help investors understand how climate-related risks affect the firm's cash flows and valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission emphasizes focusing on information that directly affects the firm's cash flows/value; this is consistent with recommendations (e.g., Fin. Economists Roundtable) and is intended to help investors make investment and voting decisions. Climate-related impacts on future cash flows may be more informative than current cash flow disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and mandatory reporting for comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many institutional investors and commenters support standardized and mandatory reporting of climate-related information so disclosures are comparable across firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys cited show investor demand for standardized/mandatory reporting; fragmentation of voluntary frameworks creates comparability challenges that mandatory standards aim to reduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-specific questions and metrics to aid comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Frameworks and questionnaires (e.g., CDP) include sector-specific questions and data points intended to aid comparability and ensure comprehensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sector-specific metrics help investors compare registrants within industries; CDP and other frameworks align with recommendations like TCFD to support sectoral comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accessibility of questionnaire/disclosure responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Some disclosure systems (e.g., CDP) allow respondents to mark answers as 'Public' or 'Private'; public responses are available at no cost to the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public responses improve transparency and accessibility; Commission staff noted the number of companies that respond to CDP but do not publicly disclose is negligible according to CDP officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveats on dataset coverage and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Data sources used for analysis (e.g., Refinitiv, Moody's AI review, CDP) have coverage limitations that may under- or overstate reporting statistics relative to the full population of registrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refinitiv covers over 88% of global market capitalization but may not track all disclosures; coverage skews toward larger firms (e.g., Russell 3000), so estimates can be understated if Refinitiv misses disclosures or overstated because smaller firms (outside its universe) are less likely to report emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy concerns with third-party vendor estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Investors and commenters report that third-party vendor data and estimation methodologies can lack accuracy and sometimes under-estimate actual emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some investors purchase third-party vendor data and note that when companies do not disclose, vendors estimate across industries based on proactive peers; commenters express concern about lack of accuracy and the under-estimation tendency of estimation methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of robust matching/validation methods for datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: When matching voluntary questionnaire respondents (e.g., CDP) to registrants, matching on ticker, company name (e.g., using Levenshtein distance), and manual review should be used to ensure alignment with SIC codes and industry descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission staff matched CDP respondents to registrants using ticker and name-matching then manually reviewed industry alignment; such methods improve the reliability of analyses based on external datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assurance performed in accordance with professional assurance standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Assurance services designed to provide assurance should be performed in accordance with professional standards (e.g., AICPA, PCAOB); verification services may not be designed to provide assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assurance differs from verification; many assurance engagements reported in studies are limited assurance rather than reasonable assurance. The Commission notes the distinction and the importance of professional standards to provide credible assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate assurance provider qualifications and applicable standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-CPA assurance providers may not be able to use AICPA or PCAOB attestation standards; many non-accountant providers instead reference other standards (e.g., ISO 14064-3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies report that non-CPA assurance reports are common and often reference standards other than AICPA/PCAOB; the Commission notes evidence that some assurance providers are not applying AICPA standards, and that non-CPAs cannot use those attestation standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of assurance should be disclosed and interpreted
rubrics_metrics.description: Assurance engagements vary in the level of assurance provided (e.g., limited, reasonable), and stakeholders should be able to distinguish these levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IFAC study cited: among large firms, the majority of assurance was 'limited assurance' with fewer obtaining 'reasonable assurance'; assurance reports sometimes reference multiple standards; percentages and distinctions should be transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider firm size in disclosure and assurance expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Larger firms are more likely to follow frameworks (SASB, GRI, TCFD, CDP) and to obtain third-party assurance than smaller registrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics show higher adoption rates among larger half of Russell 1000 versus smaller half; rule design and expectations should account for disparities in capacity and current practice across firm sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to standard sector classification systems for context
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of standard sector classification systems (e.g., MSCI's GICS) is appropriate when discussing sector categories for disclosure and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites MSCI GICS as source for sector categories; standardized sector classifications support cross-company comparisons and sector-specific reporting.
